c.tagline: Danube fortress city of student energy, Habsburg streets, and Europe's biggest music festival.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered and cheap by Western standards; confirm the meter is running or agree a price beforehand, especially from the bus or train station.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-style number that reaches police, fire, and ambulance and is increasingly recommended, especially for foreigners.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets on crowded buses and in EXIT Festival crowds; otherwise usual awareness.

hood_desc: Novi Sad's pedestrian-friendly historic core around Freedom Square, the Name of Mary Church, and City Hall; best for first-time visitors who want museums, cafes, and nightlife all within walking distance.

The fortress town across the Danube, home to the massive Petrovaradin Fortress and clock tower and the site of the EXIT Festival each July; suits history lovers and festival-goers wanting river views and cobblestone streets.
A leafy 1960s-80s district of university buildings, parks, and the Štrand river beach along the Danube; good for families, students, and travelers wanting green space and a quieter pace.
A modern business and shopping district south of downtown with malls, offices, and newer apartment blocks; suits travelers who prioritize shopping and contemporary conveniences over historic charm.

A traditional low-rise neighborhood turned canvas for street art and murals, with a growing cluster of galleries and indie cafes; suits younger travelers and art enthusiasts wanting an authentic, less touristy feel.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: Buses generally run from about 4:30-5:00 AM until around midnight; there is no dedicated night network.
transit.pay: Fares are paid with a prepaid rechargeable BusPlus card tapped on boarding, or a slightly higher cash fare paid to the driver.
transit.note: 21 urban and 35 suburban lines are operated by the public company JGSP Novi Sad; the city's old tram network was decommissioned in 1957 and never replaced.

air: No airport in Novi Sad itself; nearest is Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport (BEG)
train: Regional trains toward Subotica and Hungary
bus: Intercity buses from Novi Sad Bus Station

transit.m: Bus/shuttle plus onward bus or train to Novi Sad

tip.r: Not expected but rounding up or leaving 5-10% at restaurants for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Fis paprikas (Danube fish stew)
food.desc: Vojvodina's signature paprika-red river-fish stew, simmered in a cauldron over open fire with catfish, carp and pike, served with noodles.

places.name: Carda Aqua Doria
places.note: Riverside fish czarda famous for cauldron fis paprikas and live tamburica bands.

places.name: Fish i Zelenis
places.note: Long-running Novi Sad fish kitchen, small menu of river fish done well.

places.name: Salas 137
places.note: Working Vojvodina farmstead restaurant, classic fish stew and horse-drawn carriage rides.

food.name: Sarma
food.desc: Sour-cabbage leaves rolled around minced pork and rice, slow-baked with smoked ribs; the winter table centrepiece all over Vojvodina.

places.name: Plava Frajla
places.note: Nostalgic Vojvodina dining room; sarma and stuffed vine leaves are the house specialities.

places.name: Sokace
places.note: Homestyle Serbian tavern often singled out by visitors for the best sarma in town.

places.name: Kod Fazana
places.note: Neighbourhood kafana cooking old Vojvodina recipes at local prices.

food.name: Karadjordjeva snicla
food.desc: The 'maiden's dream' - a rolled, breaded veal or pork schnitzel stuffed with kajmak and fried golden, served with tartar sauce.

places.name: Restoran Veliki
places.note: Old-school city restaurant, a reliable benchmark for Serbian meat classics.

places.name: Plava Frajla
places.note: Generous version with proper kajmak, in a room full of vintage Novi Sad photos.

places.name: Sokace
places.note: Traditional kitchen just off Zmaj Jovina, good value main courses.

food.name: Strudla (walnut and poppy-seed strudel)
food.desc: Paper-thin rolled pastry filled with ground walnuts, poppy seed or sour cherries - the Austro-Hungarian legacy in every Vojvodina kitchen.

places.name: Salas 84
places.note: Farmhouse restaurant where the strudel is still stretched and rolled by hand.

places.name: Salas 137
places.note: Homemade strudel and knedle finish the long Vojvodina lunch here.

places.name: Futoska pijaca
places.note: Market bakers sell trays of walnut and poppy strudel every morning.

food.name: Knedle sa sljivama
food.desc: Potato-dough dumplings wrapped around whole plums, boiled then rolled in buttery toasted breadcrumbs and sugar.

places.name: Salas 137
places.note: Plum dumplings made to the old farmhouse recipe, best in late summer.

places.name: Plava Frajla
places.note: Retro dining room that keeps grandmother-style Vojvodina desserts on the menu.

places.name: Lipov Lad
places.note: Leafy restaurant across the Danube popular with families for homemade sweets.

food.name: Rostilj: cevapi and pljeskavica
food.desc: Skinless minced-meat fingers and a wide grilled patty, served in lepinja flatbread with raw onion, ajvar and kajmak.

places.name: Restoran Kafanica
places.note: Busy central kafana turning out grilled meat platters late into the evening.

places.name: Kod Fazana
places.note: Charcoal grill favoured by locals rather than tourists.

places.name: Dunavska and Zmaj Jovina street grills
places.note: Cluster of walk-up rostilj windows for a cheap late-night cevapi lepinja.

food.name: Fruska Gora wine and Bermet
food.desc: Hillside vineyards south of the city make crisp Rizling and red Probus, plus Bermet, the spiced fortified dessert wine of Sremski Karlovci.

places.name: Vinarija Kovacevic
places.note: One of Serbia's best-known estates, tastings 30 minutes from Novi Sad.

places.name: Podrum Bajilo
places.note: Family cellar in the historic wine town, the classic place to taste Bermet.

places.name: Laze Teleckog street wine bars

food.name: Rakija
food.desc: Homemade fruit brandy - sljivovica from plums, dunja from quince, kajsija from apricot - poured as a welcome and a farewell.

places.note: Long list of house rakijas to open a Vojvodina meal.

places.name: Laze Teleckog street

places.name: Salas 137

landmarks: Petrovaradin Fortress
The 'Gibraltar of the Danube' looms over the river with eighteenth-century bastions, an upside-down clock tower and the EXIT festival each July.
Trg Slobode (Liberty Square)
Novi Sad's grand central square pairs the neo-Renaissance City Hall with the Name of Mary Church beneath the Miletić monument.
The Name of Mary Church
This neo-Gothic Catholic church's 72-meter spire and Zsolnay-tiled roof dominate Liberty Square, glowing colorfully at dusk.
Dunavska Street and Zmaj Jovina
The old town's pedestrian arteries wind between pastel Habsburg facades, cafés and courtyards from Liberty Square toward the Danube Park.
Dunavski Park (Danube Park)
A romantic nineteenth-century park of weeping willows, busts and a swan pond, the city's beloved green drawing room.
Štrand Beach
Novi Sad's famous Danube river beach draws thousands each summer to its sandy shore, pools of café terraces and fortress views.
Fruška Gora National Park and Monasteries
The wooded holy mountain south of town shelters sixteen Serbian Orthodox monasteries, vineyards and hiking trails within an easy day trip.
Sremski Karlovci
A jewel-box baroque town twenty minutes away, cradle of Serbian culture, famous for its cathedral, old gymnasium and bermet dessert wine.
Museum of Vojvodina
Two adjoining palaces chart the multicultural Pannonian plain from prehistory onward, starring three gilded late-Roman parade helmets.
Novi Sad Synagogue
A monumental Hungarian Art Nouveau synagogue from 1909 on Jevrejska Street, now a haunting concert hall honoring the city's Jewish heritage.

intl.to: Budapest (Hungary) - change at Subotica for the cross-border local train to Szeged and a Hungarian InterCity onward

train.note: Novi Sad's rebuilt station on Bulevar Jaše Tomića is a stop on the modernised Belgrade-Subotica high-speed line, where 200 km/h Soko trains cover the 75 km to Belgrade in about 35 minutes and reach Subotica in well under an hour. The Budapest link reopened on 8 October 2025 but is not yet a through train: you change at Subotica onto a local across the border to Szeged and then a Hungarian InterCity to Budapest, and the two railways sell the legs separately. The direct Zagreb-Belgrade train remains suspended, so Croatia is a bus journey. Soko seats are reserved and cheapest booked a few days ahead at https://www.srbvoz.rs/.

intl.to: Budapest (Hungary), Vienna (Austria), Munich (Germany), Zagreb (Croatia) & Sarajevo (Bosnia and Herzegovina)

bus.note: The central bus station is at Bulevar Jaše Tomića 6, immediately beside the railway station and about 2 km from the old town, with frequent local buses and taxis into the centre. Lasta (https://www.lasta.rs/) issues e-tickets by email and runs both regional services into Croatia and long-haul coaches to Western Europe, while FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) covers Budapest, Vienna and the Balkan capitals; counters at the station sell the same journeys in cash. Serbia is outside Schengen and the EU, so the Hungarian and Croatian crossings involve a full passport check that can add an hour or more at busy times, and buses to Zagreb (about 5-6 hours from Belgrade) are currently the only public transport on that corridor.

ferry.note: Novi Sad stands on the Danube but has no scheduled passenger ferry or river-bus service - the bridges carry all cross-river traffic. The quay below Petrovaradin is used by international river cruise ships working the Passau-Budapest-Belgrade route, which call here on itineraries rather than selling point-to-point passage, plus seasonal sightseeing boats.

half.name: Belgrade
half.blurb: Serbia's capital, with Kalemegdan Fortress and the Skadarlija bohemian quarter, is about an hour away by train or highway.

half.name: Subotica
half.blurb: An Art Nouveau town hall and synagogue near the Hungarian border sit roughly ninety minutes north of Novi Sad.

half.name: Bač
half.blurb: A restored medieval fortress and a former Franciscan monastery stand on the Bačka plain about an hour away.

half.name: Zrenjanin
half.blurb: This Banat river town has Austro-Hungarian architecture along the Begej River, roughly an hour east of Novi Sad.
